1. The frames show a grid of small houses. Each house stands for one historical US starting period, and the legend says what its lighting means. A lit house means the buyer was ahead after ten years. A dark house means the renter was ahead. The data sources named on screen are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The animation is labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE" and "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. The houses get lit or dark as the animation goes on. In frame 1 the left rows are already lit and a patch in the middle is dark. In frames 3 to 5 a new diagonal strip of lit houses appears among the dark ones. The camera then tilts into a top-down view in frame 6. There the left block is mostly lit, the middle is mixed with dark squares, and the right block is mostly dark.

3. In this history, buying beat renting over ten years in many periods, shown by the large lit block on the left. In other periods renting came out ahead, shown by the dark blocks in the middle and right. So the result depended on when someone started, because prices, rents and mortgage rates differed from one period to the next. Neither choice won every time.

4. A viewer could take away that buy-versus-rent isn't settled in either direction. The outcome has varied by period, and a ten-year horizon seems to matter. The viewer might also decide to run their own numbers with current prices, rates and rents before choosing. The frames give no specific instruction, and I can't read the exact share of lit versus dark houses from them.

5. The picture and on-screen text didn't give that advice. The animation only shows the lit and dark pattern and the disclaimers "history, not a forecast" and "illustrative." The advice in 4 is my own conclusion from the pattern.
